topic: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Sound waves (physics only) (HT only)
subject: physics

items.q: A sound wave from a loudspeaker passes through a brick wall and is heard in the next room. What happens inside the wall as the sound passes through it?
items.correct: The particles of the brick vibrate, passing the wave through the solid
items.misconception: The wave travels through tiny air gaps between the brick particles
items.why: Students picture the wave as a moving object that must find a path, and particle diagrams drawn with spaces between the circles suggest gaps that air could occupy. It also lets them keep the belief that sound only really travels in air. There is no separate 'sound' passing through gaps. The wave is the vibration: the particles of the solid vibrate about their positions and pass the vibration to their neighbours, so the solid as a whole is set vibrating.
items.random_wrong: The wave stops at the wall because sound can only travel in air

items.q: Which statement best describes how sound waves cause the sensation of sound in the ear?
items.correct: Sound waves make the ear drum and other parts of the ear vibrate
items.misconception: Nerves in the ear respond to the wave without anything vibrating
items.why: Students know hearing ends up as something the brain interprets, and biology lessons emphasise nerves and the brain. The physical, mechanical middle step is skipped, so the limit is attributed to the brain rather than to the vibrating solid parts. The specification's chain is mechanical: sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, and that vibration causes the sensation of sound. Because the conversion into vibrations of solids only works over a limited frequency range, the limits of hearing are set before any signal reaches the brain.
items.random_wrong: The ear drum only vibrates when a sound is loud enough to hear

items.q: The cone of a loudspeaker is made to move in and out rapidly and a sound is heard. Which conversion is taking place at the cone?
items.correct: Vibrations of a solid are converted into sound waves in the air
items.misconception: Sound waves in the air are converted into vibrations of a solid
items.why: The ear drum is the example students meet first and it is always used in the sound-to-vibration direction, so the reverse process is never rehearsed - even though loudspeakers and every struck or plucked object are examples of it. Both directions occur. A microphone diaphragm is set vibrating by sound waves; a loudspeaker cone vibrates and pushes on the air to send out sound waves. The specification asks for processes which convert wave disturbances between sound waves and vibrations in solids - between, so either way.
items.random_wrong: Sound waves are converted into electrical signals inside the cone

items.q: A microphone contains a thin diaphragm. A student speaks into the microphone. What happens at the diaphragm first?
items.correct: Sound waves in the air make the solid diaphragm vibrate
items.misconception: The diaphragm vibrates first and then creates sound waves
items.why: The ear drum is the example students meet first and it is always used in the sound-to-vibration direction, so the reverse process is never rehearsed - even though loudspeakers and every struck or plucked object are examples of it. Both directions occur. A microphone diaphragm is set vibrating by sound waves; a loudspeaker cone vibrates and pushes on the air to send out sound waves. The specification asks for processes which convert wave disturbances between sound waves and vibrations in solids - between, so either way.
items.random_wrong: The sound wave passes through gaps in the diaphragm

items.q: A signal generator and loudspeaker produce a sound at 30 kHz at very high volume. A student with normal hearing hears nothing. Why?
items.correct: The conversion of the wave into vibrations does not work at that frequency
items.misconception: The sound is not loud enough for the ear drum to be able to vibrate at all
items.why: Loudness is the everyday variable students control - volume knobs, moving closer, shouting. Amplitude and frequency are easily conflated, so 'cannot hear it' is read as 'not loud enough' rather than 'the wrong frequency to be converted'. Loudness and frequency are different properties. A 30 kHz sound played at very high volume is still not heard, because the ear drum and other parts of the ear do not convert a wave of that frequency into vibrations at all.
items.random_wrong: At 30 kHz the loudspeaker is not producing a sound wave at all

items.q: The range of normal human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Written in hertz, what is the upper limit of this range?
items.why: The prefix kilo is handled loosely, and students remember the pair of numbers '20 and 20' without securing which unit each carries. Multiplying by 100 or by 10 000 feels no less arbitrary than multiplying by 1000. Kilo always means one thousand: 20 kHz = 20 x 1000 Hz = 20 000 Hz. The range of normal human hearing is therefore 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz - a factor of a thousand between the two limits.

items.q: Which one of these frequencies lies outside the range of normal human hearing?
items.why: The upper limit is the one students hear about - ultrasound, dog whistles, losing high frequencies with age. Very low frequencies are rarely demonstrated, so the 20 Hz end of the range is remembered as a starting point rather than as a genuine limit. The range is bounded at both ends because the conversion into vibrations of solids fails at both ends. A 15 Hz wave is a sound wave, but it lies below 20 Hz and is outside the range of normal human hearing.

items.q: One student taps the far end of a long metal railing. Another student, with an ear against the railing, hears the tap clearly. Which statement explains this?
items.correct: The tap sets the metal vibrating and the vibrations travel along it
items.misconception: Sound cannot travel in metal at all, so it must have come through the air
items.why: Students meet sound first as 'waves in air' and are taught that sound cannot travel through a vacuum. 'Needs a medium' is then compressed to 'needs air', and everyday experience of walls muffling sound reinforces the idea that solids stop sound rather than carry it. A sound wave needs a material to travel through, and a solid is a material. In a solid the particles are close together and pass the vibration on very readily, which is why a tap at one end of a metal rail is heard clearly at the other end.
items.random_wrong: The sound travels through gaps in the metal without moving it

items.q: Why does the conversion of sound waves into vibrations of solids only work over a limited frequency range?
items.correct: Solid parts such as the ear drum will only vibrate over a limited range
items.misconception: Only sounds above a certain loudness can make any solid vibrate
items.why: Loudness is the everyday variable students control - volume knobs, moving closer, shouting. Amplitude and frequency are easily conflated, so 'cannot hear it' is read as 'not loud enough' rather than 'the wrong frequency to be converted'. Loudness and frequency are different properties. A 30 kHz sound played at very high volume is still not heard, because the ear drum and other parts of the ear do not convert a wave of that frequency into vibrations at all.
items.random_wrong: Sound waves only exist over a limited range of frequencies

items.q: The ear drum and other parts of the ear can be made to vibrate only within a limited range of frequencies. What does this fact explain?
items.correct: Why human hearing has an upper and a lower frequency limit
items.misconception: Why very quiet sounds cannot be heard at any frequency
items.why: Loudness is the everyday variable students control - volume knobs, moving closer, shouting. Amplitude and frequency are easily conflated, so 'cannot hear it' is read as 'not loud enough' rather than 'the wrong frequency to be converted'. Loudness and frequency are different properties. A 30 kHz sound played at very high volume is still not heard, because the ear drum and other parts of the ear do not convert a wave of that frequency into vibrations at all.
items.random_wrong: Why sounds outside human hearing are not really waves

items.q: Is a 30 kHz wave a sound wave?
items.correct: Yes. It is a sound wave; it simply lies outside the range over which the human ear can convert sound into vibrations.
items.misconception: If nobody can hear it, it is not a sound - sound waves only exist between 20 Hz and 20 kHz.
items.why: The 20 Hz to 20 kHz figures are learned as a fact about sound rather than as a fact about human ears, so the limits of the detector are mistaken for limits of the wave. 20 Hz to 20 kHz is the range of normal human hearing, not the range of sound. Waves above and below those frequencies are still sound waves and still make solids vibrate; they are just not converted by the human ear.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
